cim: When Excellence Becomes Evidence of Artificial Intelligence
cim_eredeti: When Excellence Becomes Evidence of Artificial Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
Imagine a student who submits an essay of unusual distinction. The argument is ambitious, the prose exact and the connections between apparently remote subjects illuminating. Her teacher, who has never expected quite so much of her, sends it to an artificial intelligence system to discover whether another artificial intelligence system wrote it. A procedure ostensibly designed to protect human achievement begins with the suspicion that this particular human cannot have achieved so much. The better the work, the more urgently its author must explain herself.

There is a circularity here which deserves closer attention than the familiar complaint that detection software sometimes makes mistakes. We train machines upon human expression, teach them to reproduce its virtues and then ask machines to decide which instances of those virtues remain credibly human. Their answers acquire authority through the very capabilities which made the question difficult. Eventually, a civilisation may find that it has given artificial intelligence the power to define the permissible limits of human intelligence.

Some distinctions are necessary. An AI detector may be a specialised classifier trained upon labelled examples, a statistical test or a system looking for a deliberately embedded watermark. It need not be a conversational large language model. Nor is there anything logically absurd about using computation to investigate computational activity. A detector tested against independently established authorship can supply useful evidence. The circle becomes dangerous when an institution treats a model’s impression of authorship as if it were independent knowledge of how the work came into existence.

Asked whether it wrote an unfamiliar passage, a language model does not ordinarily gain access to the passage’s history merely by reading it. Unless it has relevant records or other evidence, its answer must rest upon inference from the material presented. It may produce an elegant explanation involving sentence structure, transitions and vocabulary. Yet an explanation of resemblance is not an observation of origin. A human author can write something a machine could have written, just as a machine can reproduce something a human actually wrote.

This difficulty has a mathematical expression. Research by Vinu Sankar Sadasivan and colleagues connects the limits of text detection to the statistical distance between human and machine output. As those distributions approach one another, even the best detector has less information with which to separate them. This is a conditional limit, rather than proof that every existing detector is worthless. Nevertheless, it exposes the ambition behind universal detection: to recover a difference in causal history from a finished object which may no longer contain a reliable trace of that difference.

The vocabulary of error matters. Taking a positive result to mean a finding of AI generation, a false positive occurs when human work is wrongly classified as machine work. A true negative occurs when human work is correctly recognised as human; it is a successful result, not an error. A false negative is machine work mistakenly accepted as human, while a true positive correctly identifies machine work. The troubling question is what kinds of human achievement will continue to receive the reassuring true negative, and what writers will learn to sacrifice in order to obtain it.

Even apparently modest error rates can become serious when applied indiscriminately. Suppose, purely as an illustration, that 100 of 10,000 submissions are machine-generated. A detector which identifies 90 per cent of those while falsely flagging just 1 per cent of the human submissions produces 90 correct accusations and 99 incorrect ones. More than half its positive findings are wrong. The institution announcing a small false-positive rate may therefore be running a process in which an accused person is more likely to be innocent than guilty.

There is already evidence of unequal exposure to suspicion. In a 2023 study, Weixin Liang and colleagues tested seven detectors upon 91 human-authored TOEFL essays by non-native English writers. The average false-positive rate exceeded 60 per cent. These were particular tools and samples at a particular time, rather than a measurement of every detector available today. Their importance lies in what they revealed: an apparently neutral assessment of authorship could penalise a linguistic characteristic shared by an identifiable group of human writers.

For a Ukrainian scholar writing in English, or any author working outside her first language, such mistakes can turn participation in international intellectual life into a peculiarly exhausting exercise. She must satisfy the substantive demands of her discipline while also anticipating what a classifier considers a plausible human style. A device sold as an instrument of academic integrity may introduce a second, unofficial examination, conducted according to criteria which the candidate cannot meaningfully inspect.

False negatives create a different pressure. If institutions demand that fewer machine texts escape, they may lower the threshold for suspicion and thereby accuse more humans. Meanwhile, generators and their users can adapt to the characteristics being detected. Sadasivan and colleagues demonstrated that repeated paraphrasing substantially weakened several detection methods, sometimes with only modest deterioration in the text. A detector’s success against a fixed collection of outputs does not establish equivalent success against an adversary who can change his procedure.

The evidence also contains a useful corrective to sweeping pessimism. A 2025 working paper by Brian Jabarian and Alex Imas found strong performance by several commercial detectors, with Pangram achieving near-zero error rates within their tested material. That result deserves acknowledgement. It shows that detection can work well under specified conditions. It does not settle how a tool will treat every unfamiliar genre, future model or exceptional author, and a population-level success rate still requires care when translated into an accusation against an individual.

There is also uncertainty about what the accusation means. A person may devise an argument, write its first version and ask a model to improve the grammar. Another may commission the entire argument and alter a few words. Both texts contain machine contributions, but their intellectual histories differ profoundly. A 2025 study by Shoumik Saha and Soheil Feizi found that detectors frequently flagged even minimally polished human writing and struggled to distinguish degrees of AI involvement. A binary verdict can conceal precisely the distinction an institution ought to be investigating.

None of this establishes that present detectors systematically identify brilliance as artificial. Some of the clearest evidence concerns the misclassification of comparatively simple or predictable language. The prediction about exceptional thinkers concerns a further development: what happens when increasingly capable machines meet institutions which already distrust achievement beyond their expectations. The statistical defects of a detector and the social assumptions of its users can reinforce one another without being identical.

The premise that large language models are already more intelligent than humans requires some precision about the comparison. In important intellectual tasks they have already reached levels beyond the overwhelming majority of people. In 2025, an advanced version of Gemini Deep Think achieved the gold-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad, with its solutions officially graded by the competition’s coordinators. That does not establish superiority to every human across every dimension of thought. It does establish that exceptional intellectual performance can no longer serve as a reliable presumption
